content: The accuracy of point-of-care (POC) HBV DNA assays, including their sensitivity and specificity, was compared to laboratory-based nucleic acid testing (NAT). A total of 15 studies involving 8,791 participants were analyzed. Six of these studies evaluated the Xpert HBV DNA assay, while the remaining nine assessed other laboratory-based POC assays, such as the HBV-LAMP Assay, Duplex real-time RAA, HBV-MCDA-LFB Assay, and Cas12a-DETECTR Assay. Plasma was used exclusively in six studies, serum or plasma in seven studies, and whole blood in two studies. Four studies utilized fresh samples, while eight used frozen samples. When compared to a laboratory-based reference standard, the pooled sensitivity and specificity of the Xpert assay were 96% (95% CI: 94–98%) and 98% (95% CI: 90–100%), respectively. Similarly, other POC assays demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy, with pooled sensitivity and specificity of 98% (95% CI: 94–99%) and 99% (95% CI: 93–100%), respectively. The certainty of the evidence was rated as moderate to high. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended the use of POC molecular assays for rapid identification of rifampicin-resistant and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) and for routine TB diagnosis. In 2021, WHO also endorsed POC RNA assays for early infant diagnosis of HIV and routine viral load monitoring in individuals living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART). These recommendations were based on high-certainty data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and large, well-characterized cohorts. POC early infant diagnosis testing for HIV was associated with faster result delivery and quicker ART initiation, with infants being eight times more likely to start treatment within 60 days of sample collection. Similarly, POC HIV RNA testing for viral load monitoring resulted in faster result return and clinical action compared to standard-of-care methods. A systematic review of 45 studies on hepatitis C virus (HCV) care found that POC testing for HCV RNA reduced the time from antibody testing to treatment initiation and increased uptake of RNA testing and treatment, particularly among marginalized populations with high rates of loss to follow-up, such as people who inject drugs. This evidence, rated as moderate-certainty, supports the use of POC platforms to reduce delays between testing and clinical decision-making for treatment initiation. The WHO Guidelines Development Group acknowledged the limited access to laboratory-based HBV DNA NAT assays in resource-limited settings due to high costs and infrastructure requirements, which pose significant barriers to treatment uptake. The increased availability of POC platforms for HIV, TB, and during the COVID-19 pandemic presents an opportunity to expand access to HBV DNA assays. Based on moderate to high-certainty evidence, the group conditionally recommended the use of POC NAT assays as an alternative to laboratory-based NAT assays for measuring HBV DNA, given their high diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity: 96–98%; specificity: 98–99%). A systematic review of seven studies found that POC DNA testing was associated with high uptake of viral load testing (89%, 95% CI: 55–100%) and treatment initiation (88%, 95% CI: 66–100%) among eligible individuals. The time from testing to result return and treatment initiation ranged from one to eight days, with fewer healthcare facility visits. However, this evidence was rated as very low-certainty due to serious risk of bias and indirectness, as only one study included a non-POC comparison group. Key benefits of POC HBV DNA assays include their ability to be decentralized to lower-level healthcare facilities due to ease of use and single-test capability. They can expand access for HBV treatment eligibility assessment or antiviral prophylaxis among pregnant women with high viral loads at risk of transmitting hepatitis B to their offspring, as well as for monitoring treatment response. This is particularly valuable in hard-to-reach settings and communities with limited access to laboratory-based services or sample transport systems. POC platforms are already in use for other infectious diseases, such as HIV monitoring, early infant diagnosis, and TB diagnosis, and their integration into existing platforms could expand access to HBV DNA and HCV RNA testing. Challenges of POC testing include limited test throughput compared to laboratory-based platforms, requiring prioritization of testing in high-demand settings. There are few manufacturers of POC HBV NAT assays, limiting competition and cost reduction. Additionally, some assays, such as Xpert, require high-temperature incineration for safe disposal of guanidinium thiocyanate-containing waste. A multicountry survey of over 400 individuals with hepatitis B highlighted preferences for testing and treatment delivery. Key priorities included confidentiality of test results, access to knowledgeable staff, appropriate counseling, non-stigmatizing approaches, minimizing costs, and convenient testing locations. Respondents emphasized the importance of POC NAT assays as an option due to cost and availability barriers to HBV DNA testing. POC HBV DNA assays can promote equity by addressing high-risk populations prone to loss to follow-up, such as pregnant women in antenatal care, prisoners, and people who inject drugs at harm-reduction sites. The introduction of multi-disease testing devices offers opportunities for integration, expanding access, and achieving system efficiency and cost savings. Countries with existing multi-disease platforms for HIV, TB, or HCV can consider integrating HBV DNA testing into these systems. Operational considerations for POC testing include the need for decentralized systems with quality control, platform maintenance, supply chain management, trained personnel, and proper waste disposal. Basic laboratory infrastructure, such as centrifuges, POC devices, and temperature-controlled environments, is essential. Regular quality assurance checks and personnel training are necessary to ensure proper use of POC devices. Storage and transport conditions for POC cartridges must be carefully managed to maintain assay integrity. The optimal placement of POC instruments is at sites where testing and treatment are co-located, minimizing delays and additional costs associated with travel to separate facilities. For HCV care, POC assays have been most effective when integrated into one-stop-shop models, particularly for marginalized populations. However, this model may be less applicable to hepatitis B care, as many individuals may meet treatment eligibility without requiring an HBV DNA assay. In summary, POC HBV DNA assays offer significant potential to improve access to testing and treatment in resource-limited settings, but their implementation requires careful consideration of operational, logistical, and equity-related factors.
